strengths: Well-motivated real-world problem addressing a genuine bottleneck in spectroscopic survey vetting with clear motivation and impact
Thoughtful alignment of model design with expert astronomer workflow (iMCoT), potentially improving trust and transparency over black-box classifiers

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including five rare-object tasks, cross-survey generalization (LAMOST→SDSS/DESI), cross-task zero-shot transfer, and well-designed SpecVI-Bench with rejection-sampled hard negatives
Strong empirical results with ~48 percentage-point F1 improvement over base model (28.3%→76.5%) and impressive cross-survey stability despite instrumental differences
Rigorous human evaluation by six Ph.D. astronomers validating reasoning quality (coherence/physical consistency) with strong agreement to LLM judges and parity with proprietary o3
Practical two-stage training strategy (SFT+RL) leverages the real-world scenario of scarce demonstrations but abundant labels
Thorough ablation studies (Table 4) demonstrating importance of both training stages and tool access, with clear contribution analysis
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: iMCoT is natural to the problem, SFT+GRPO RL is standard practice; contribution is primarily in application rather than methodology, reducing impact for an NLP-focused venue
Narrow scope with acknowledged limitations—only 5 rare-object types, no coverage of broader spectral subclasses or challenging observational conditions; generalization claims overstated
Incomplete modeling of real-world vetting workflow: abstracts as pure spectral inspection, ignoring cross-database matching, photometry, imaging, time-domain evidence required in actual surveys

Cold-start barrier for deployment: requires ~1k expert-curated trajectories per new task/object type with labor-intensive curation pipeline (guidelines→draft→revision→dual-audit→vote), limiting scalability
Critical production-readiness gaps: explicitly lacking calibration, abstention mechanisms, risk controls, confidence thresholds, and computational cost analysis—essential for real survey deployment

Weak statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; cross-survey evaluation on small matched datasets (~300 samples); macro-F1 averaging masks per-class performance; incomplete coverage (SS, WD unsupported)
Insufficient failure analysis: no error case studies, expert disagreement analysis, confusion matrices, or systematic discussion of failure modes limiting trustworthiness assessment
Hard-negative construction via rejection sampling (1.74% acceptance) creates artificial distribution; unclear how performance generalizes to production conditions with different priors
Comparison fairness concerns: specialist baselines fine-tuned differently; comparing VLM+tool to pure classifiers is not entirely apples-to-apples; no ablation isolating tool contribution

Reproducibility issues: 'Project HomePage' vague (no concrete URL); depends on specific Qwen2.5-VL versions; GPT-5 generation step uses non-public models; expert curation involves subjective judgment limiting protocol reproducibility; α parameter not stated in main text

strengths: Well-motivated real-world problem: Addresses a genuine bottleneck in modern spectroscopic surveys where expert manual inspection cannot scale with data growth
Strong empirical results: Macro-F1 improvement from 28.3% to 76.5%, outperforming proprietary o3 (52.3%) and specialized deep learning baselines with good cross-survey/cross-task robustness
Rigorous experimental design: Proper ablations demonstrating necessity of both SFT and RL stages, hard-negative construction via rejection sampling, and careful dataset construction
Comprehensive human evaluation: Expert astronomers (Ph.D. requirement) validate reasoning coherence and physical consistency with custom annotation interface
Interpretability focus: Emphasis on reasoning trajectories addresses legitimate trust concerns with deep learning in scientific domains
Thorough evaluation protocol: Multiple datasets, cross-survey generalization tests, cross-task transfer, preference studies, and analysis of training dynamics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contributions are incremental applications of existing methods—iMCoT framework inspired by o3, visualization tool is straightforward wavelength slicing, training uses standard GRPO without architectural innovations. Better characterized as domain application than methodological advance

Critical reproducibility barrier: Requires extensive expert annotation (3 astronomers per trajectory) for cold-start with no quantified effort cost. Extending to new domains requires re-doing expert guideline formulation and trajectory curation. Scalability claims undermined by expert dependence

Insufficient error analysis: Only 100/many-thousand trajectories evaluated; no failure case analysis; 10-30% F1 variance across tasks (especially WD at 53.6%) unexplained; high 46% tie rate in preference study suggests weak signal

Overclaimed generalization: Cross-survey only covers 3/5 tasks; cross-task is to O/B/A stellar types (same paradigm) still requiring reformulated expert guidelines; no transfer to fundamentally different spectroscopic problems or discovery paradigms

Dataset and baseline concerns: Hard negatives from weak classifier with 1.74% acceptance rate (calibration unclear); o3 comparison may be unfair (not fine-tuned for task); no sensitivity analysis on visualization parameters; limited architectural comparisons

Incomplete methodological analysis: No ablation on reward design choices; no RL sample-efficiency comparison; no analysis of whether learned diagnostic priorities match expert priorities; sensitivity to wavelength ranges unstudied

Venue misalignment: Limited NLP/CL contribution makes it a poor fit for ACL main conference. Primary value is astronomy-domain-specific; applications of existing VLM techniques without novel methods or insights for general NLP community

Evaluation scope limitations: Only 6 expert raters with no inter-rater reliability (ICC/κ) reported; reasoning quality rubric conflates coherence with correctness without astronomical ground-truth validation; cold-start trajectories hybrid human-GPT-5 data of unclear representativeness

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine bottleneck (manual spectral vetting) in modern astronomy with clear practical significance
Principled domain alignment: system design mirrors authentic astronomer workflows (global view → iterative local zoom), enhancing both trustworthiness and performance

Comprehensive, rigorous experimental evaluation: strong in-distribution results (76.5% vs 28.3% baseline), impressive cross-survey generalization (81.1% SDSS, 77.4% DESI vs 56.1% for o3), and cross-task transfer (76.4% on unseen spectral types)
Rigorous benchmark design (SpecVI-Bench) with realistic hard negatives via rejection sampling rather than stratified sampling, plus imbalanced test sets reflecting true target rarity

Outstanding human expert validation: 6 Ph.D. astronomers evaluated reasoning quality with high inter-rater consistency; pairwise preference study shows Spec-o3 preferred over o3; validation directly addresses trustworthiness motivation
Comprehensive ablations convincingly demonstrate necessity of both SFT and RL stages, and tool access (20.7 point drop without tools)

Clear, well-structured presentation with excellent figures (especially Figure 2 on iMCoT), detailed appendices, honest limitations section, and strong reproducibility support (promised code/data/models, training details provided)
Addresses fundamental interpretability concern: demonstrates that transparent, tool-assisted reasoning can match/exceed opaque black-box models on a scientific task
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty for ML/NLP audience: interleaved reasoning inspired by o3, two-stage SFT+RL is standard practice, GRPO is existing work (Shao et al. 2024), uses pre-trained Qwen2.5-VL. Contribution is primarily application + evaluation rather than novel methods

Significant cold-start data requirements (1k expert trajectories with multi-stage review) create practical barriers; no exploration of minimizing requirements, knowledge transfer across tasks, or trajectory-count vs. performance curves

Potentially unfair comparison with o3: o3 received no task-specific fine-tuning on LAMOST data, while Spec-o3 leverages 1k SFT trajectories + RL. Comparison doesn't isolate whether architectural advances or training data drives improvements. Fairer baseline would be o3 fine-tuned on cold-start data

Problem formulation simplified relative to real catalog construction: abstracted as binary zoom-and-reason on spectra alone, but real workflows require cross-database matching, multi-modal data (photometry, imaging, time-domain), and contextual information. Acknowledged but unaddressed

Missing production-oriented features essential for real deployment: no confidence calibration, no abstention mechanism for uncertain cases, no expert-triage strategy—all critical given expert bandwidth constraints
Incomplete failure analysis: WD task shows much lower F1 (53.6% vs 81.0% for CV)—why? No confusion matrices, systematic error patterns, or analysis of when tool calls most benefit reasoning

Generalization testing lacks statistical rigor: cross-survey evaluation uses small matched samples (~50 positives, 250 negatives per task); no confidence intervals, significance tests, or per-task reliability reporting

Tool utility mechanism unclear: 20.7 point F1 drop without tools (55.8% vs 76.5%), but analysis doesn't isolate whether benefit derives from attention focus, better feature rendering, scaffolded reasoning, or other factors

Dataset size and pre-training overlap concerns: only ~3.4k training samples on small domain-specific distribution; limited analysis of how much performance comes from Qwen's pre-training vs. task-specific adaptation

Hyperparameter and design choices underspecified: reward function parameter α (Eq. 3) value not stated; GRPO learning rates and schedules partially missing; max tool calls (8) limit frequency not analyzed; sensitivity analyses absent

Cross-task generalization scope limited: O/B/A-type stars use same prompt format and tool interaction paradigm; true generalization would involve fundamentally different inspection procedures, not just different feature sets
Human evaluation scale modest: 100 trajectories sampled; no discussion of statistical power, multiple-comparison correction, or inter-rater variability beyond correlation coefficients

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical impact: Addresses genuine bottleneck in large-scale spectroscopic survey workflows with ~50× throughput gain
Methodology naturally aligns with expert workflows: iMCoT approach mirrors actual astronomer inspection patterns (global view → iterative zooming)
Rigorous experimental evaluation: Comprehensive generalization testing across surveys (LAMOST→SDSS/DESI), tasks (O/B/A-types), and extreme cases (QSO, low-SNR); proper handling of class imbalance

Strong empirical results: Achieves 76.5% macro-F1 vs. base model 28.3% (+48.2%); outperforms proprietary o3 (52.3%) and science-specialized models (42.2%); demonstrates notable zero-shot transfer (76.4% on unseen stellar types)
Interpretability validation with human experts: 100 trajectories evaluated by 6 domain experts; high coherence and physical consistency scores; LLM judge agreement supports scalable assessment
Sound two-stage training methodology: Ablations (Table 4) show both SFT and RL necessary; cold-start injection of domain priors prerequisite for effective RL optimization
High-quality data construction: SpecVI-Bench rejection sampling creates realistic high-confusion vetting scenario; expert-reviewed cold-start trajectories with consensus-based quality control
Reproducibility: Detailed appendices, promised code/data/model release, transparent experimental documentation supporting independent verification
weaknesses: Limited task scope reduces generalizability: Only 5 rare-object types evaluated (all from LAMOST); real catalogs involve 20+ classes; cross-task generalization tested on only 3 stellar types (O/B/A)

Expert annotation bottleneck limits scalability: Cold-start requires ~1k trajectories; synthetic trajectory generation (Appendix J) only demonstrated on QSO; scaling to new surveys/types remains uncertain

Incomplete workflow coverage: Paper automates only spectral inspection, not full vetting (missing cross-matching, photometry/imaging/time-domain evidence incorporation); framing as 'end-to-end' somewhat overstated

Generalization performance not uniformly strong: Cross-task F1 drops 5-15 points on unseen types; QSO subset shows 71.9% vs. 76.5% in-distribution; claims of 'strong generalization' partially unsubstantiated

Limited baseline comparisons for broader context: Recent think-with-image competitors (Mini-o3, GRIT, VLM-R3) cited but not directly compared on SpecVI-Bench; unfair comparison with screening-stage DL baselines
Small-scale human evaluation: Only 100 of ~1000 test trajectories evaluated by 6 experts; limited statistical coverage of reasoning quality assessment

Simple reward function lacks refinement: Binary outcome-based reward (Eq. 3) with no intermediate rewards for tool efficiency, reasoning quality, or confidence calibration; ablation on reward design absent
Insufficient error analysis: No discussion of failure modes, misclassifications, or reasoning errors; understanding when/why model fails would aid deployment
Synthetic trajectory quality underexplored: Dependence on LLM generator + filtering (Gemini-2.5-Pro) not analyzed; no comparison of performance trained on synthetic vs. human-authored trajectories
Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple-run variance reported; results presented as point estimates without uncertainty quantification

strengths: Addresses a genuine practical bottleneck in astronomical surveys with well-motivated application of tool-augmented reasoning
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple generalization dimensions (cross-survey, cross-task, extreme cases) with rigorous human expert evaluation
Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over baselines and unexpected robustness properties (e.g., 78.2% F1 at SNR<5)
Thoughtful experimental design including token-level loss masking to prevent overfitting, detailed ablation studies, and interpretable training dynamics analysis
Well-executed domain application with clear practical value (~50× speedup) and transparent reasoning that supports expert trust
weaknesses: Primarily a domain application paper with limited relevance to computational linguistics/NLP; applies established techniques (multimodal CoT, tool-augmented agents, GRPO) rather than proposing novel CL methodology
Substantial cold-start annotation requirement (~1k expert trajectories per task) with expensive multi-round auditing process is downplayed; this is a significant barrier to deployment
Incomplete consideration of full vetting pipeline: lacks integration with external databases, multi-modal evidence, and production-grade risk controls (calibration, abstention mechanisms)
Insufficient error analysis and failure mode characterization; no systematic investigation of when model confidence is misplaced or which spectral types are problematic
Generalization claims overstated: cross-survey shifts limited to optical spectroscopy, QSO generalization still requires 96 synthetic trajectories, unclear performance on truly novel object types
Baseline comparisons somewhat unfair (specialist DL models designed for screening not vetting) and missing ablation of fine-tuned VLM without tool-augmentation
Evaluation limited to custom dataset (SpecVI-Bench) with no external validation or out-of-distribution testing; hard negatives from rejection sampling may not reflect true contaminant distributions
Reproducibility concerns: relies on proprietary models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude) for trajectory generation and evaluation; exact prompts not fully specified
